1	//! Per-resource authorization — *what* an authenticated caller may touch.
2	//!
3	//! [`crate::auth`] answers *who* the caller is ([`Principal`]); this module is
4	//! the decision function and the enforcement points. It exists because of
5	//! issue #79: a brain used to be isolated **by name only**, so any credential
6	//! that could reach the node could read, write and destroy every brain.
7	//!
8	//! ## The rule, in one sentence
9	//!
10	//! The `.xerj-memory-*` index namespace — every agent-memory namespace and
11	//! every second brain — is **reserved**: reaching it requires a principal that
12	//! holds the matching privilege on the specific index, and the only principals
13	//! that hold anything there are the superuser and a key explicitly granted the
14	//! index by name.
15	//!
16	//! ## The mistake this file is built to make impossible
17	//!
18	//! The first cut of #79 decided against the index named in the **URL path**.
19	//! That is not the index several handlers operate on. `_msearch` takes it from
20	//! an NDJSON header line, `_bulk` from an action line, `_mget` from
21	//! `docs[]._index`, `_aliases` from its action list, `_reindex` from
22	//! `source`/`dest`, a `terms` lookup and a `lookup` runtime field from deep
23	//! inside a query, an index template from a *pattern* that will match brains
24	//! created later, `_sql` from the table name in the statement — in every one of
25	//! those the path index is only a *default* that the body overrides. Four of
26	//! them were proven live against a running node: read another tenant's brain
27	//! through `_msearch`, forge and delete its edges through `_bulk`, read a
28	//! document through `_mget`, and launder a whole index into reach by pointing
29	//! an alias at it.
30	//!
31	//! A per-handler patch list would have closed those four and left the fifth.
32	//! So authorization is decided at two places that no handler can route around:
33	//!
34	//! 1. **Here, before the handler runs.** [`authz_middleware`] resolves the
35	//!    complete target set of a request — from the path *and* from the body —
36	//!    resolves aliases to concrete indices, and authorizes each one with the
37	//!    privilege the request actually needs. This produces the precise
38	//!    ES-shaped 403 and gets read-vs-write-vs-manage right.
39	//! 2. **In the engine, at the point the name becomes an index.**
40	//!    [`xerj_engine::index_guard`] installs the request's principal as a
41	//!    task-local visibility rule that `Engine::get_index`,
42	//!    `get_or_create_index`, `create_index`, `delete_index`,
43	//!    `list_indices` and `index_name_list` all consult. A handler cannot
44	//!    forget this check, because a handler does not call it — it is inside the
45	//!    only funnel to index data. Anything the first layer did not know to look
46	//!    for (a body shape added next year, an `_sql` table name, a scroll
47	//!    context) still fails closed there.
48	//!
49	//! Layer 2 answers "not found" rather than "forbidden", deliberately: it makes
50	//! a denied brain indistinguishable from an absent one, and it means fan-out
51	//! (`POST /_search`, `_cat/indices`, `logs-*`) *filters* instead of failing —
52	//! which is what lets the global verbs keep working for ordinary credentials
53	//! instead of being refused wholesale.
54	//!
55	//! ## Enforcement points (all of them)
56	//!
57	//! | Door | Enforced by |
58	//! |---|---|
59	//! | `POST /_graph/{brain}/link` | `graph_api::link` + middleware |
60	//! | `DELETE /_graph/{brain}/link/{edge_id}` | `graph_api::unlink` + middleware |
61	//! | `GET /_graph/{brain}/ego` | `graph_api::ego` + middleware |
62	//! | `GET /_graph/{brain}/overview` | `graph_api::overview` + middleware |
63	//! | `POST/GET/DELETE /_memory/{ns}[/…]` (the brain's *nodes* index) | `memory_api` + middleware |
64	//! | any ES-compat route naming a reserved index in the path | middleware |
65	//! | any route naming an index in its **body** (`_bulk`, `_msearch`, `_mget`, `_aliases`, `_reindex`, snapshot `indices`, `terms` lookups, `lookup` runtime fields, `POST /v1/indices`) | middleware ([`body_targets`]) |
66	//! | an index template whose `index_patterns` would own a brain's mapping | middleware ([`authorize_template_patterns`]) |
67	//! | an ML job/datafeed config naming the index the server will go and read | middleware ([`BodyShape::MlConfig`]) |
68	//! | the detached datafeed scorer `_start` spawns | `es_compat::spawn_datafeed_task`, carrying the starter's rule across the `tokio::spawn` |
69	//! | an **alias** pointing into the reserved namespace | middleware (resolved before the decision) + `Engine::get_index` (resolved before the guard) |
70	//! | index patterns (`logs-*`, `_all`, `*`) | expanded only over the principal's visible set ([`xerj_engine::index_guard`]) |
71	//! | unnamed fan-out (`POST /_search`, `/_bulk`, `/_all/*`) | authorized per named index; anything unnamed is filtered by the guard |
72	//! | enumeration (`GET /_mapping`, `/_cat/indices`, `/_resolve/index/*`) | filtered at `Engine::list_indices`, then pruned in the response |
73	//! | the native router's `/v1/indices/{name}/…` spelling of the same index | middleware ([`Target::Indices`] classifies both routers) |
74	//! | the native router's body-named create (`POST /v1/indices`) | middleware ([`BodyShape::NativeCreate`]) |
75	//! | the gRPC listener (`:8081`) | `xerj-server::grpc`, using [`Principal::allows_index`] |
76	//! | privilege escalation via `POST /_security/api_key` | `es_compat::security_create_api_key` |
77	//! | anything else that resolves an index name from anywhere | `xerj_engine::index_guard` |
78	//!
79	//! ## Fail-closed
80	//!
81	//! Matching the precedent set elsewhere in the tree (a corrupt sidecar, an
82	//! unknown marker version and an unsatisfiable doc all refuse rather than
83	//! guess), every unresolved case here denies:
84	//! - an unknown/expired/invalidated credential → [`Principal::Denied`] → deny;
85	//! - a key minted with no usable `role_descriptors` → [`Principal::Unscoped`]
86	//!   → **no** privilege on the reserved namespace;
87	//! - an unrecognized ES privilege name → grants nothing;
88	//! - a body this module must parse to find its target but cannot → deny;
89	//! - a snapshot or restore that names no indices (i.e. *all* of them,
90	//!   including brains) → superuser only;
91	//! - an index expression that resolves to nothing this principal can see →
92	//!   resolves to nothing, not to everything.
93	//!
94	//! ## What this does **not** claim
95	//!
96	//! Broad RBAC over the general ES-compat surface is still deferred: an
97	//! `Unscoped` key keeps its historical superuser-equivalent reach over
98	//! *ordinary* indices. This module makes the reserved namespace a real
99	//! boundary and confines a `Scoped` key to its grants; it does not turn xerj
100	//! into a general multi-tenant authorization system. `xerj_engine::rbac`'s
101	//! named `RoleStore` remains unenforced data.
102	//!
103	//! Nor does it second-guess an explicit grant. A scoped key minted with
104	//! `names: ["*"]` **can** read the reserved namespace, because `*` matches
105	//! every index and that is what the operator asked for; only a superuser can
106	//! mint one. See [`xerj_engine::rbac::Role::applies_to`] for the reasoning and
107	//! `a_star_grant_reaches_the_reserved_namespace` below for the pinned
108	//! behaviour. Operators who want brain isolation must grant concrete names or
109	//! a prefix that excludes `.xerj-memory-`.
110	
111	// The decision functions return `Result<(), Response>` where `Err` IS the
112	// ready-to-send 403. That trips `clippy::result_large_err` (an `axum::Response`
113	// is a fat value), but boxing it would add an allocation on the deny path to
114	// satisfy a lint aimed at hot `Ok` paths, and would obscure that the error
115	// *is* the response.
116	#![allow(clippy::result_large_err)]

164	/// reserved namespace?
165	///
166	/// Deliberately conservative in the deny direction: a pattern is judged by the
167	/// literal text before its first `*`, and if that prefix is a prefix of — or is

169	/// `*`, `_all`, `.*`, `.xerj-*` and `.xerj-memory-alice*` all qualify;
170	/// `logs-*` does not.
171	///
172	/// Read patterns are no longer *refused* on the strength of this — they are
173	/// expanded over the principal's visible set instead, which is both safe and
174	/// the only way a granted `logs-*` can work. It is still what decides whether
175	/// a name a caller is about to *create* (an alias, a fresh index) is squatting
176	/// the reserved namespace.
177	pub fn may_reach_reserved(expression: &str) -> bool {
178	    let expr = expression.trim();
179	    if expr.is_empty() {
180	        return false;
181	    }
182	    if expr == "_all" {
183	        return true;
184	    }
185	    let head = expr.split('*').next().unwrap_or("");
186	    if expr.contains('*') {
187	        head.starts_with(RESERVED_INDEX_PREFIX) || RESERVED_INDEX_PREFIX.starts_with(head)
188	    } else {
189	        is_reserved_index(expr)
190	    }
191	}

194	fn is_pattern(expr: &str) -> bool {
195	    expr.contains('*') || expr == "_all"

203	///
204	/// Ordered before any existence check on purpose: an unauthorized caller gets
205	/// the same 403 whether or not the resource exists, so 403-vs-404 cannot be
206	/// used to enumerate brains.
207	pub fn authorize_index(
208	    principal: &Principal,
209	    index: &str,
210	    privilege: Privilege,
211	) -> Result<(), Response> {
212	    if principal.allows_index(index, privilege) {
213	        Ok(())
214	    } else {
215	        Err(forbidden(principal, index, privilege))

217	}

220	///
221	/// Deliberately **not** routed through [`Principal::allows_index`]: audit read
222	/// is not index-scoped, and that predicate answers `true` for an `Unscoped` key
223	/// on any non-reserved name — which is exactly the hole this closes. The audit
224	/// log is one object covering the whole node, holding every tenant's activity
225	/// and every security event, so "reach over ordinary indices" is not a reason
226	/// to be handed it.
227	///
228	/// Two principals hold it: the superuser, and a key minted with
229	/// `cluster: ["read_audit"]` (see
230	/// [`xerj_engine::rbac::roles_from_role_descriptors`]). An `Unscoped` key —
231	/// one minted with no `role_descriptors` — does not, and neither does a key
232	/// scoped to indices, however broad the grant: `names: ["*"]` is an *index*
233	/// grant and says nothing about the audit log.
234	pub fn holds_audit_read(principal: &Principal) -> bool {
235	    match principal {
236	        Principal::Superuser => true,
237	        Principal::Scoped { roles, .. } => roles
238	            .iter()
239	            .any(|r| r.privileges.contains(&Privilege::AuditRead)),

249	/// middleware also short-circuits the superuser before it classifies anything,
250	/// so a cluster-level check does not belong there.

284	        Privilege::ReadIndex => "read",
285	        Privilege::WriteIndex => "write",
286	        Privilege::AdminIndex => "manage",
287	        Privilege::SnapshotCreate => "create_snapshot",

304	            "action [{action}] is unauthorized for this credential on [{resource}]: mint a key \

306	             use the configured admin key"
307	        )

310	        principal = principal.label(),
311	        resource,
312	        action,
313	        "authorization denied"

462	/// Split a URI path into percent-decoded, non-empty segments.
463	fn segments(path: &str) -> Vec<String> {
464	    path.split('/')
465	        .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
466	        .map(percent_decode)
467	        .collect()
468	}
469	
470	/// Minimal percent-decoder. The middleware compares raw path text against
471	/// index names, so `%2Exerj-memory-alice-edges` must not slip past a check
472	/// that `.xerj-memory-alice-edges` would fail. Invalid escapes are left
473	/// verbatim (they cannot decode into the reserved prefix).
474	fn percent_decode(s: &str) -> String {
475	    if !s.contains('%') {
476	        return s.to_string();
477	    }
478	    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
479	    let mut out: Vec<u8> = Vec::with_capacity(bytes.len());
480	    let mut i = 0;
481	    while i < bytes.len() {
482	        if bytes[i] == b'%' && i + 2 < bytes.len() {
483	            let hex = std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[i + 1..i + 3]).ok();
484	            if let Some(b) = hex.and_then(|h| u8::from_str_radix(h, 16).ok()) {
485	                out.push(b);
486	                i += 3;
487	                continue;
488	            }
489	        }
490	        out.push(bytes[i]);
491	        i += 1;
492	    }
493	    String::from_utf8_lossy(&out).into_owned()
494	}

496	/// Classify a request path.
497	fn classify(path: &str) -> Target {
498	    // Probes, the scrape endpoint, and "who am I" — none of which name or
499	    // reveal an index. `_security/_authenticate` in particular must stay open
500	    // to a scoped key, or a caller cannot verify its own credential.
501	    if AUTH_EXEMPT_PATHS.contains(&path)
502	        || path == "/v1/metrics"
503	        || path == "/_security/_authenticate"
504	        // `POST /_share/claim` is unauthenticated by design (the guest
505	        // has no key yet) and names no index; the handler decides everything.
506	        || crate::auth::is_share_claim_path(path)
507	    {
508	        return Target::Exempt;
509	    }
510	    let segs = segments(path);
511	    let Some(first) = segs.first() else {
512	        // `GET /` — the version banner. No data.
513	        return Target::Exempt;
514	    };
515	    match first.as_str() {
516	        "_graph" => match segs.get(1) {
517	            Some(brain) => Target::Brain(brain.clone()),
518	            // No brain in the path: no route matches, let it 404.
519	            None => Target::Exempt,
520	        },
521	        "_memory" => match segs.get(1) {
522	            Some(ns) => Target::Memory(ns.clone()),
523	            None => Target::Exempt,
524	        },
525	        // Native router (`build_native_router`, :8080). Same engine, same
526	        // indices, different spelling — and therefore the same boundary:
527	        // `GET /v1/indices/.xerj-memory-alice-edges` must be no more reachable
528	        // than `GET /.xerj-memory-alice-edges`.
529	        "v1" => match (segs.get(1).map(String::as_str), segs.get(2)) {
530	            (Some("indices"), Some(expr)) | (Some("schema"), Some(expr)) => {
531	                Target::Indices(split_expressions(expr), 3)
532	            }
533	            // `POST /v1/indices` names its index in the body — authorized as
534	            // `BodyShape::NativeCreate`, not refused for lack of a path target.
535	            _ => Target::Cluster,
536	        },
537	        // `/_all/_search` and `/*/_search` are index-scoped routes whose index
538	        // happens to be a pattern — not cluster endpoints. Classifying them
539	        // here is what lets them expand over the caller's visible set like any
540	        // other pattern instead of being refused for naming nothing.
541	        s if s == "*" || s == "_all" => Target::Indices(split_expressions(s), 1),
542	        s if s.starts_with('_') => Target::Cluster,
543	        s => Target::Indices(split_expressions(s), 1),
544	    }
545	}

556	/// The privilege a request needs on whatever it targets.
557	///
558	/// Conservative by construction: anything not recognized as a read or a
559	/// lifecycle op is treated as a write, so an unclassified mutation can never
560	/// be waved through as a read.
561	fn required_privilege(method: &Method, segs: &[String], op_start: usize) -> Privilege {
562	    if method == Method::GET || method == Method::HEAD {
563	        return Privilege::ReadIndex;
564	    }
565	    match segs.get(op_start).map(String::as_str) {
566	        Some(o) if POST_READ_OPS.contains(&o) => Privilege::ReadIndex,
567	        Some(o) if ADMIN_OPS.contains(&o) => Privilege::AdminIndex,
568	        // No op segment at all: the request targets the index itself, so it is
569	        // creating or destroying it.
570	        None => Privilege::AdminIndex,
571	        _ => Privilege::WriteIndex,
572	    }
573	}

577	/// `GET`/`HEAD` always do. So does any verb whose op is one of the read ops:
578	/// `POST /_search`, `/_count`, `/_msearch`, `/_mget` are the reason the global
579	/// verbs are usable at all, and `DELETE /_search/scroll` / `DELETE /_pit` /
580	/// `DELETE /_async_search/{id}` release a session the caller already opened.
581	fn cluster_is_read(method: &Method, segs: &[String]) -> bool {
582	    if method == Method::GET || method == Method::HEAD {
583	        return true;
584	    }
585	    match segs.first().map(String::as_str) {
586	        Some(op) => POST_READ_OPS.contains(&op),
587	        None => true,

591	/// The privilege a `/_graph/{brain}/…` or `/_memory/{ns}[/…]` request needs.
592	///
593	/// Kept separate from [`required_privilege`] because these paths spell their
594	/// ops without a leading underscore (`link`) and because deleting a whole
595	/// namespace is a lifecycle op while deleting one document is not.
596	fn reserved_api_privilege(method: &Method, segs: &[String]) -> Privilege {
597	    if method == Method::GET || method == Method::HEAD {
598	        return Privilege::ReadIndex;
599	    }
600	    if method == Method::POST {
601	        // `POST /_memory/{ns}/_recall` reads; `POST /_memory/{ns}` and
602	        // `POST /_graph/{b}/link` write. Creating the backing index lazily is
603	        // part of writing a brain, not a separate `manage` step.
604	        return if segs.iter().any(|s| s == "_recall") {
605	            Privilege::ReadIndex
606	        } else {
607	            Privilege::WriteIndex
608	        };
609	    }
610	    if method == Method::DELETE {
611	        // `DELETE /_memory/{ns}` drops the whole namespace → manage.
612	        // `DELETE /_memory/{ns}/{id}` and `DELETE /_graph/{b}/link/{id}` are
613	        // document-level → write.
614	        return if segs.len() <= 2 {
615	            Privilege::AdminIndex
616	        } else {
617	            Privilege::WriteIndex
618	        };
619	    }
620	    Privilege::WriteIndex
621	}

1043	/// Middleware that sets ES-compatible product headers on every response.
1044	///
1045	/// Kibana and other Elastic clients verify the presence of `X-Elastic-Product`
1046	/// before trusting the response. A real OpenSearch server never sends this
1047	/// header at all, so a caller detected (or forced, see
1048	/// [`es_compat::is_opensearch_caller`]) as OpenSearch must NOT receive it —
1049	/// some OpenSearch-ecosystem clients treat an unexpected product header as
1050	/// just another response header, but there's no reason to send an
1051	/// Elastic-specific identity marker to a client we've already decided isn't
1052	/// Elastic. A `Warning` header is included for Elastic callers only, for the
1053	/// same reason.
1054	///
1055	/// A real OpenSearch server also sends `X-OpenSearch-Version: OpenSearch/<n>
1056	/// (opensearch)` on every response, verified against a real OpenSearch 3.7.0
1057	/// container — an OpenSearch-detected caller gets the equivalent header
1058	/// here, built from the same version xerj already reports in `GET /`'s
1059	/// `version` block (`es_compat::resolve_compat_version`), so the two stay in
1060	/// sync by construction. Found missing while chasing an OpenSearch
1061	/// Dashboards Timeline (Timelion) panel that rendered empty against xerj but
1062	/// correctly against real OpenSearch for the byte-identical aggregation
1063	/// response body — this header was the one structural difference between
1064	/// the two.
1065	async fn es_headers_middleware(
1066	    State(state): State<AppState>,
1067	    req: Request,
1068	    next: Next,
1069	) -> Response {
1070	    let is_opensearch = es_compat::is_opensearch_caller(&state, req.headers());
1071	    let opensearch_version =
1072	        is_opensearch.then(|| es_compat::resolve_compat_version(&state, req.headers()).number);
1073	    let mut resp = next.run(req).await;
1074	    let headers = resp.headers_mut();

1	//! Share links — hand one indexed corpus to someone who has nothing else.
2	//!
3	//! `xerj brain <folder>` leaves the owner with a node whose only credential is
4	//! the admin key. Sending a friend that key hands them the whole node; minting
5	//! them a scoped key by hand means explaining `role_descriptors`. A share is
6	//! the one-command version of the second thing: the owner names an index (and
7	//! optionally the brain whose links sit beside it), gets a link plus a
8	//! passcode, and the guest who opens the link and types the passcode is
9	//! handed a **scoped, read-only, expiring** API key that reaches exactly the
10	//! indices the share names — and nothing else on the node.
11	//!
12	//! ## What is stored, and what is not
13	//!
14	//! Records live in `<data_dir>/shares.json` beside `api_keys.json` — same 0600
15	//! atomic writer ([`xerj_engine::engine::write_secret_file_atomic`]). They are
16	//! deliberately *not* documents in a reserved index: a file is reachable by no
17	//! search, `_cat`, snapshot, alias or `_delete_by_query` route, so there is no
18	//! second copy of the reserved-namespace exception list to keep in sync.
19	//!
20	//! Nothing in a record is a usable secret:
21	//! - the share id (the token in the link) is stored as a **SHA-256 digest**;
22	//!   the plaintext exists only in the create response and in the link;
23	//! - the passcode is stored as an **Argon2id** hash. Unlike a minted API-key
24	//!   secret (244 bits of CSPRNG, see `xerj_engine::secret_hash` for why that
25	//!   one is a fast hash) a passcode is short and may have been chosen by a
26	//!   human, so an offline guess is a real threat and a slow hash is the right
27	//!   tool. It is verified once per claim, on a rate-limited route, so the cost
28	//!   never lands on the request path;
29	//! - the guest's API key is **minted at claim time**, one per claim, expiring
30	//!   when the share expires. The record keeps only the minted key *ids* so a
31	//!   revoke can invalidate every key the share ever produced. No credential
32	//!   is ever written to the share file.
33	//!
34	//! ## Who may do what
35	//!
36	//! | Route | Who |
37	//! |---|---|
38	//! | `POST /_share`, `GET /_share`, `DELETE /_share/{handle}` | superuser only (the admin key) — a scoped or unscoped key gets 403 |
39	//! | `POST /_share/claim` | **nobody in particular** — it is exempt from authentication (`auth::is_share_claim_path`) the way `/v1/metrics` is for the scrape token, and rate-limited per source address and per share instead |
40	//!
41	//! The claim route is the only unauthenticated door that hands out a
42	//! credential, so it is narrow on purpose: one exact path, `POST` only, a body
43	//! capped at [`MAX_CLAIM_BODY_BYTES`], a sliding-window throttle,
44	//! `Cache-Control: no-store` on every answer, and every outcome — success,
45	//! wrong passcode, exhausted, expired, revoked, unknown, throttled — in the
46	//! audit log with the source address.
47	//!
48	//! ## The share id is never part of a request path
49	//!
50	//! The claim body is `{id, passcode}`. The first cut put the id in the path
51	//! (`POST /_share/{id}/claim`), and the guest page's care to keep the id in the
52	//! URL *fragment* was undone one request later: a request path is exactly what
53	//! an access log records. With `logging.access_log = true` this node wrote the
54	//! id to `server.log` twice per claim, and any reverse proxy or tunnel in front
55	//! of it logged the same line (review of PR #947, reproduced 2026-09-19). A
56	//! body is in none of those logs. `DELETE /_share/{handle}` takes the public
57	//! handle, which opens nothing. It also accepts the full id, for an API caller
58	//! who kept only that — such a call puts the id in its own request path, which
59	//! is why `xerj share --revoke` sends only the handle.
60	//!
61	//! ## The two throttles, and why a tunnel does not break them
62	//!
63	//! - A claim against a **known** share is charged to that share's window
64	//!   ([`SHARE_PER_MINUTE`] / [`SHARE_PER_HOUR`]), from anywhere. This is the
65	//!   passcode lockout, and it does not depend on knowing who is asking.
66	//! - A claim against an **unknown** id is charged to the source address's
67	//!   window ([`IP_PER_MINUTE`] / [`IP_PER_HOUR`]). It bounds junk traffic and
68	//!   the audit lines it writes.
69	//!
70	//! They are deliberately *not* stacked. The first cut charged the source
71	//! window before looking the share up, which is fine on a directly exposed
72	//! node and wrong behind `xerj share --tunnel`: every request a tunnel (or any
73	//! reverse proxy on the same host) delivers arrives from `127.0.0.1`, so all
74	//! guests shared one source bucket, and ten junk requests a minute from anyone
75	//! who had found the hostname answered every real guest with `429` — a
76	//! one-line denial of service on the feature. The fix is not to believe
77	//! `X-Forwarded-For`: a direct client writes that header itself (#76 S5-4),
78	//! and an unconfigured node believes nobody. It is to stop the collapsed
79	//! bucket from mattering: a real share id is governed by its own window, which
80	//! no amount of junk can touch, and junk is governed by the source window,
81	//! where collapsing every tunnel client into one bucket only makes the bound
82	//! tighter.
83	//!
84	//! Operators who want each guest's real address — in the audit log and as the
85	//! junk-traffic key — declare the proxy the usual way,
86	//! `server.trusted_proxies = ["127.0.0.1", "::1"]`; then, and only then,
87	//! `X-Forwarded-For` is read, right to left (see [`ClaimSource`]). IPv6
88	//! sources are keyed by their /64, since one host is routinely handed a whole
89	//! /64 to rotate through.
90	//!
91	//! ## An open node cannot share
92	//!
93	//! With authentication off (`--insecure`, `auth.enabled = false`, or no admin
94	//! key) every request is [`Principal::Superuser`], so a "scoped, read-only"
95	//! guest key would restrict nothing. `POST /_share` and the claim route answer
96	//! `409` there rather than hand out a credential that promises a boundary the
97	//! node is not enforcing.
98	//!
99	//! ## What a guest can reach
100	//!
101	//! The minted key carries one role, named `share:<handle>`: `read` on the
102	//! share's `indices` plus, when a brain is named, `read` on that brain's edges
103	//! index (`authz::brain_edges_index`). Two things then confine it:
104	//!

106	//!    gets, in the middleware and again in the engine's index funnel;
107	//! 2. a **route allow-list** that applies to share guests only
108	//!    (`authz::guest_route_allowed`, keyed on [`GUEST_ROLE_PREFIX`]):
109	//!    `_search`, `_count`, `_msearch`, `_mget`, `_mapping`, `_field_caps` and
110	//!    `GET _doc/{id}` on the granted indices, and
111	//!    `GET /_graph/{brain}/ego|overview`. An ordinary scoped key is given a
112	//!    *filtered* view of `_cat`, `_cluster/*`, `_nodes` and friends because
113	//!    Kibana needs one; a guest is given none of it. No `scroll`, no `_pit`,
114	//!    no `_async_search` either — nothing that parks state on the owner's
115	//!    machine.
116	//!
117	//! The `autoindex-catalog` index is **never** granted, and cannot be named in a
118	//! share ([`CATALOG_INDEX`], refused by `validate_share_index`): it lists every
119	//! corpus on the node, the engine has no document-level security to filter it
120	//! with, and the guest page already receives the index name directly.
121	//!
122	//! Every response to a guest key is `Cache-Control: no-store`
123	//! (`authz::authz_middleware`): it is somebody's documents, on its way through

396	    /// Charge one claim attempt against `key`. `Err` when over either window.
397	    /// Same sliding-window shape as the console's auth limiter
398	    /// (`xerj-console-api::auth::rate_limit`), re-implemented here because
399	    /// that one is bound to `ConsoleState` and this crate must not depend on
400	    /// the console.
401	    fn charge(
402	        &self,
403	        key: &str,
404	        per_minute: u32,
405	        per_hour: u32,
406	        now_ms: u64,
407	    ) -> Result<(), Throttled> {
408	        use std::sync::atomic::Ordering;
409	        if self
410	            .charges
411	            .fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)
412	            .is_multiple_of(PRUNE_EVERY)
413	        {
414	            self.windows
415	                .retain(|_, w| now_ms.saturating_sub(w.start_ms) < WINDOW_HOUR_MS);
416	        }
417	        // Bounded state for an unauthenticated route: once the table is full,
418	        // addresses it has not seen yet are throttled as one.
419	        // Only source keys collapse: share keys are bounded by the number of
420	        // shares, which only the superuser can create.
421	        let key = if key.starts_with("ip:")
422	            && self.windows.len() >= MAX_WINDOWS
423	            && !self.windows.contains_key(&format!("{key}:m"))
424	        {
425	            "ip:overflow"
426	        } else {
427	            key
428	        };
429	        for (suffix, window_ms, limit) in [
430	            ("m", WINDOW_MIN_MS, per_minute),
431	            ("h", WINDOW_HOUR_MS, per_hour),
432	        ] {
433	            let k = format!("{key}:{suffix}");
434	            let mut w = self.windows.entry(k).or_insert(RateWindow {
435	                count: 0,
436	                start_ms: now_ms,
437	            });
438	            if now_ms.saturating_sub(w.start_ms) > window_ms {
439	                *w = RateWindow {
440	                    count: 0,
441	                    start_ms: now_ms,
442	                };
443	            }
444	            w.count = w.count.saturating_add(1);
445	            if w.count > limit {
446	                return Err(Throttled {
447	                    retry_after_secs: (w.start_ms + window_ms).saturating_sub(now_ms) / 1000 + 1,
448	                    first_in_window: w.count == limit + 1,
449	                });
450	            }
451	        }
452	        Ok(())
453	    }
454	}

491	/// Alphabet for generated passcodes: lowercase + digits with the four
492	/// look-alikes (`0/o`, `1/l`, plus `i`) removed, 31 symbols. Eight of them is
493	/// ~39.6 bits, which with [`SHARE_PER_HOUR`] guesses an hour is out of reach
494	/// online, and which is what the human on the other end has to type.
495	const PASSCODE_ALPHABET: &[u8] = b"abcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz23456789";
496	
497	/// `xxxx-xxxx` from the alphabet above.
498	pub fn generate_passcode() -> String {
499	    let mut out = String::with_capacity(9);
500	    let mut rng = rand::rngs::OsRng;
501	    for i in 0..8 {
502	        if i == 4 {
503	            out.push('-');
504	        }
505	        // Rejection-free: 31 does not divide 256, so draw a u32 and take the
506	        // modulo of a much larger range; the bias is < 2^-24 per symbol.
507	        let n = rng.next_u32() as usize % PASSCODE_ALPHABET.len();
508	        out.push(PASSCODE_ALPHABET[n] as char);
509	    }
510	    out
511	}

532	fn hex(bytes: &[u8]) -> String {
533	    const T: &[u8; 16] = b"0123456789abcdef";
534	    let mut s = String::with_capacity(bytes.len() * 2);
535	    for b in bytes {
536	        s.push(T[(b >> 4) as usize] as char);
537	        s.push(T[(b & 15) as usize] as char);
538	    }
539	    s
540	}

542	fn constant_time_eq(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool {
543	    if a.len() != b.len() {
544	        return false;
545	    }
546	    let mut diff = 0u8;
547	    for (x, y) in a.iter().zip(b) {
548	        diff |= x ^ y;
549	    }
550	    diff == 0
551	}

567	/// `"30m"`, `"24h"`, `"7d"` (and `"90s"`) → milliseconds. `None` on anything
568	/// else, including a bare number: the unit is the whole point.
569	pub fn parse_expires_in(spec: &str) -> Option<u64> {
570	    let s = spec.trim();
571	    let split = s.find(|c: char| c.is_ascii_alphabetic())?;
572	    let (num, unit) = s.split_at(split);
573	    let n: u64 = num.trim().parse().ok()?;
574	    let per_ms: u64 = match unit.trim() {
575	        "d" => 86_400_000,
576	        "h" => 3_600_000,
577	        "m" => 60_000,
578	        "s" => 1_000,
579	        _ => return None,
580	    };
581	    n.checked_mul(per_ms)
582	}

584	/// Is `name` a concrete index a share may grant? Same alphabet the engine
585	/// accepts, minus anything that is a pattern or a list — a grant must name
586	/// exactly what it grants — and minus the reserved namespace, which is only
587	/// reachable through `brain`.
588	fn validate_share_index(name: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
589	    if name.is_empty() || name.len() > 255 {
590	        return Err("index name must be 1–255 characters".into());
591	    }
592	    if name.starts_with(crate::authz::RESERVED_INDEX_PREFIX) {
593	        return Err(format!(
594	            "index `{name}` is in the reserved .xerj-memory-* namespace; share a brain with `brain` instead"
595	        ));
596	    }
597	    // Every dot-index is the node's own: `.xerj_sessions`, `.xerj_api_tokens`,
598	    // `.xerj_passkeys` and `.xerj_magic_links` are credential stores, and
599	    // `.xerj_audit` records who connected from where. The check above named only
600	    // the memory namespace, so a share on any of these was accepted — found by
601	    // the first live run (2026-09-18), which minted a guest link onto the audit
602	    // log. A share grants a *user's* corpus, and no user index starts with a dot,
603	    // so the rule is the whole prefix rather than a list that has to be kept in
604	    // step with every system index added later.
605	    if name.starts_with('.') {
606	        return Err(format!(
607	            "index `{name}` is a system index and cannot be shared; a share names one of your own indices"
608	        ));
609	    }
610	    if name.starts_with('_') {
611	        return Err(format!("index `{name}` is not an index name"));
612	    }
613	    // The catalog describes EVERY corpus on the node. The docs said it was
614	    // "never granted" while `xerj share autoindex-catalog` minted a guest key
615	    // that read all of it (review of PR #947). A guest is handed one corpus;
616	    // the list of the others is not part of it, and there is no
617	    // document-level security to filter the list down.
618	    if name == CATALOG_INDEX {
619	        return Err(format!(
620	            "index `{name}` is the autoindex catalog: it describes every corpus on this \
621	             node, not one of them, so it cannot be shared. Share the corpus index itself \
622	             (`xerj autoindex map` lists them)"
623	        ));
624	    }
625	    for c in name.chars() {
626	        if c.is_whitespace()
627	            || matches!(
628	                c,
629	                '*' | ',' | '/' | '\\' | '?' | '"' | '<' | '>' | '|' | '#'
630	            )
631	        {
632	            return Err(format!(
633	                "index `{name}` contains `{c}`; a share names concrete indices, not patterns"
634	            ));
635	        }
636	        if c.is_ascii_uppercase() {
637	            return Err(format!("index `{name}` must be lowercase"));
638	        }
639	    }
640	    Ok(())
641	}
